newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks hit speed bump after Hashimoto remarks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks hit speed bump after Hashimoto remarks.

text.p: The scorching run staged by U.S. blue chip stocks hit a speed bump Monday when Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto suggested that Japan might engage in large-scale selling of U.S. Treasuries.
The comments jolted U.S. financial markets, which have benefited from waves of international fund inflows during their relentless climb into record territory.
Such action by Japan could spell trouble for U.S. equities by threatening the favorable interest rate climate under which stocks have flourished.
Investors reacted with a fury and the ensuing selloff whacked more than 192 points off the Dow Jones Industrial Average, the second largest loss in point terms in history.
Analysts said Hashimoto's remarks caught blue chip stocks at a time when they were especially vulnerable to a downturn, coming after a blistering 1,400 point Dow surge in little more than two months.

"This does show you the fragility of the market," said Marshall Acuff, portfolio strategist at Smith Barney. "This thing is a roller coaster right now and it's going to put some people on their guard."

Analysts were quick to point out that a decline of 200 points -- or 300 or 400, for that matter -- would not undermine the bullish tenor of the market. Even after today's loss, the Dow is up nearly 18 percent, which is better than it musters in most full years.

"The market's been up hundreds and hundreds of points in just weeks," said Scott Bleier, chief investment strategist at Prime Charter Ltd. "I think this was just an excuse for a move that was long overdue."
"There will come a point when the buyers will return," he said. "The money has not dried up."
For now, analysts expect investors will soon reassert their "buy on a dip" philosophy, one that has served as a consistent safety net for stock prices in the past.
"I don't expect this to be the start of anything big on the downside at this point," said Roy Blumberg, chief investment strategist at Josephthal Lyon & Ross.
"It's the end of the quarter and portfolio managers will try their damnedest the last couple of days of the week to see if they can buy stocks," he said.
As far as the content of Hashimoto's remarks, analysts seemed more puzzled than concerned, particularly with the weekend's benign G7 talks still fresh in their memory.

"I think it's unfortunate and really strange to have a comment like this," Acuff said. "It doesn't jibe with what came out of the G7 and it doesn't fit with what's come out of (Japan's) Ministry of Finance in the past."
